## Findings ledger
- [C1.DOC1.F1] The source documents AUKUS as a trilateral defence and security partnership announced by Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States on 15 September 2021, with Pillar I focused on Australia’s nuclear-powered submarines and Pillar II on advanced military capabilities — dim: case_identity — case: AUKUS trilateral partnership — object-time-scope: Australia, United Kingdom, and United States; announced 15 September 2021; Pillars I and II — criterion: What institutional object is being compared, and what does it cover? — anchor: "On 15 September 2021, Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States announced a trilateral defence and security partnership, known as AUKUS." — doc: aukus — confidence: high Additional support uses anchor-b: "Within ‘Pillar II’ of the agreement is the aim to develop a range of advanced military capabilities" — doc-b: aukus
- [C1.DOC1.F2] AUKUS is treated as the principal case, while Japan and South Korea are additional non-member cases examined for their engagement with Pillar II rather than as AUKUS members — dim: case_identity — case: AUKUS with Japan and South Korea as adjacent Pillar II cases — object-time-scope: Analysis extends beyond AUKUS members to Japan and South Korea; contemporary Pillar II engagement — criterion: Which actors belong to the principal case, and which are nested or adjacent cases? — anchor: "Our analysis is not only limited to AUKUS member states, but also extends to Japan and South Korea." — doc: aukus — confidence: high Additional support uses anchor-b: "Japan and South Korea—two key defence partners under Pillar II" — doc-b: aukus
- [C1.DOC1.F3] The source’s conceptual approach treats AUKUS through militarised neoliberalism, linking security institutions and alliances to market coordination, state transformation, political coalitions, technology, and capital — dim: case_identity — case: AUKUS through the militarised-neoliberalism approach — object-time-scope: Conceptual and empirical analysis of AUKUS’s geoeconomic, institutional, and social relations, with contemporary examples — criterion: How does the source define the approach used to analyse the case? — anchor: "we argue that AUKUS exists within a system of market coordination that is now linked to security institutions and specific alliances." — doc: aukus — confidence: high Additional support uses anchor-b: "In this paper, we approach AUKUS from the lens of MN." — doc-b: aukus
- [C1.DOC1.F4] The source justifies comparing cases through the shared question of how security partnerships reconnect geopolitical relations with political economy and reshape state institutions, markets, and social relations — dim: case_identity — case: AUKUS and related Pillar II partner cases — object-time-scope: AUKUS, its member states, and Japan and South Korea in the contemporary geoeconomic order — criterion: How do these cases reconnect security cooperation with economic institutions, industrial policy, and social relations? This criterion is justified because the source explicitly frames the inquiry around that nexus — anchor: "There is indeed a need to reconnect geopolitical relations between states and the underlying social forces that reshape AUKUS." — doc: aukus — confidence: high Additional support uses anchor-b: "Such forces include the market and the state, political coalitions, technology and capital, emerging business groups and key industries, as well as security apparatuses." — doc-b: aukus
- [C1.DOC1.F5] The June 2023 proposal to increase South Korea’s Eximbank statutory-capital limit and the December 2023 revised Enforcement Decree are separately identified instruments; the text does not explicitly establish that they are the same amendment or sequential stages of one instrument — dim: case_identity — case: South Korean defence-export regulatory interventions — object-time-scope: South Korea; June 2023 legislative proposal and December 2023 Enforcement Decree — criterion: Are similarly themed instruments the same institutional object? Identity remains unresolved without an explicit identity predicate — anchor: "In response to industry calls for legislative amendments, in June 2023 the government proposed to increase the lender’s statutory capital limit." — doc: aukus — confidence: high Additional support uses anchor-b: "The revised Enforcement Decree of the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act passed the National Assembly, coming into effect in December 2023" — doc-b: aukus

sections_inspected: AUKUS, bipartisanship, and the regulatory control
scope_outcomes.criterion: Identify the documented case or conceptual approach, its actors, object, place, time, boundaries, and justified comparison criteria; distinguish principal, adjacent, and institution-level cases.
scope_outcomes.basis: The source explicitly identifies AUKUS, its three member states, Pillars I and II, its militarised-neoliberalism approach, its extension to Japan and South Korea, and separate South Korean regulatory instruments.
limitations: The source is not a systematic comparison of all AUKUS member states.
The identity relationship between the June 2023 Eximbank proposal and the December 2023 Enforcement Decree is unresolved in the text.
